newsitem.title: CANADA: Potash Corp falls on Trinidad plant rumor.
newsitem.headline: Potash Corp falls on Trinidad plant rumor.

text.p: Shares of Potash Corp of Saskatchewan fell in Toronto and New York on Monday as rumors of a major Trinidad plant problem -- which the company said were erroneous -- spooked investors.
Potash shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange closed down 2 to 104 after dropping during the session to as low as 99.85. On the New York Stock Exchange, Potash was down 1-1/4 to 74-1/4.
Potash and brokerage officials said on Monday the market reacted to a report that a second leak had occurred at a PCS Nitrogen plant in Trinidad, causing C$1.3 million of damage.
However, Potash vice-president Betty-Ann Heggie said the facility suffered only one operational problem on April 3, when a power outage caused a urea supply line to rupture and release ammonia vapor.
"The plant was back up and running in 36 hours and the maximum cost to the company was US$150,000," Heggie said in a telephone interview from Saskatoon.
NatWest Securities said in a fax to investors it maintained a "buy" rating on Potash and that the plant outage would have an "insignificant impact" on the company's financial results.
"We do not believe this accident will affect POT earnings and we believe the incident only had minor impact on production in Trinidad," NatWest said.
Merrill Lynch raised its rating on the company to "accumulate" from "neutral."
Sam Kanes, an analyst with ScotiaMcleod in Toronto, said, however, that various other factors pressured fertilizer stocks on Monday, including the flooding of vast areas of northern U.S. farmland.
"You just had to look at the weekend weather -- if you were in North Dakota, it's probably the grimmest thing you've seen in your life," Kanes said.
"Roughly speaking, about two million acres have been taken off out of the 200 million or so the Americans plant, so one percent of your acreage is gone this year."

Besides the land that will be rendered useless for planting, seeding was likely to be late and fertilizer products were expected to be difficult to ship because it may be some time before rivers can be used for transport, he said.
